title_original: New York, Stanley Stellar’s Gay Eden

blocks.caption: Andy Marshall Red, 1977 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: Published by Loose Joints, Don’t Worry Boys borrows its title from a legendary New York gay club and revives the unbuttoned pleasures of the Hudson River piers, before AIDS turns the party into a wake.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Stanley Stellar .

blocks.caption: Into The Light, 1981 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: The book opens on a facsimile of a vermilion membership card: the Don’t Worry Boys Social Club “invites you to go to The Zoo,” at 421 West 13th Street. Stanley Stellar dates it, tentatively, to the late 1960s or early 1970s.

blocks.caption:
Saul Holds Mike Nomad on Morton
St Pier, Gay Pride Day, 1979 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: In 1976, the Brooklyn native took up photography and almost at once turned his lens on the gay community of the West Village, whose nights he shared.

blocks.caption:
Marsha P. Johnson on Christopher
Street, 1987 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: His pictures ran in gay skin mags, in the newspaper New York Native and in Christopher Street , a literary magazine named after the Stonewall Inn’s street, where the founding riots of gay liberation erupted in 1969 after a police raid. A regular contributor to the magazine, the novelist Andrew Holleran, author of Dancer from the Dance (1978), discovered the photographs in its pages and saw in them “the street’s answer to Robert Mapplethorpe.”

blocks.caption: Clearly Loving, 1981 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: In a New York magnetized by cruising, the street could turn the most ordinary run to the supermarket into a chance encounter. There, clothes advertised a man’s sexual role and appetites. Keys or a bandana worn on the left marked a top; on the right, a bottom. The bandana’s color spelled out the pleasures sought. Stellar is fluent in the language.

blocks.caption: Jamie Gappa, 1992 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: “We were all walking personal ads,” Holleran writes. “We were like actors going on stage even when all we wanted was a quart of milk.” In Andy Marshall Red (1977), the model nails his entrance: leaning against pitted brick, lips parted, he lets the zipper of his jacket gape open to below the navel, baring a smooth, sculpted chest.

blocks.caption: Pack of Camel, 1987 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: The grandest of these theaters lines the Hudson. For years, the derelict piers of the Lower West Side served as solarium, cruising ground and alcove, where strangers made love in stolen moments, in the shade of the sheds or in broad daylight. Holleran recalls their soaring ceilings, the lap of water against the pilings and a “majestic vacancy” that led more than one gay writer to compare them to cathedrals.

blocks.caption: Pier Upstairs, 1979 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: Beneath these naves, two young men framed by the dark jamb of a doorway embrace on the upper floor of a pier shed, against a peeling partition ( Pier Upstairs , 1979), an orange bandana poking out of the left back pocket of a pair of jeans. The “hotties in this volume,” the novelist writes, once posed among the ruins, “perched like goats on rotten timbers, presiding over the rites of Priapus.”

blocks.caption:
Gay Pride Day Christopher Street
Sidewalk, 1981 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: Stellar shows these rites unflinchingly. In Pier Sex (1978), two naked men entwined on a towel, right on the asphalt, have kept on nothing but their striped socks and work boots. Jordan Hancock, who initiated and edited the book, belongs to “the Tumblr generation,” which came to know the photographer online. As he sees it, “fucking is everywhere now,” and seeing it on a dilapidated pier is “just beautiful, not transgressive.”

blocks.caption: Cherry Grove Kiss, 1990 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: Stellar works within breathing distance, and many of his models stare straight into the lens. Alvin Baltrop, a fellow photographer and pier regular, captured bodies and ruins there from 1975 to 1986, sometimes suspended from a harness. In 1981, Stellar photographed Peter Hujar, the master of New York portraiture who also roamed the piers, his T-shirt hiked up to bare his chest against a graffitied wall. AIDS would claim him six years later.

blocks.caption: Buddy & Jimmy, NYC, 1984 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: In June 1981, the first cases of the epidemic were reported, and desire now brushed against death. Stellar moved part of the scene into the privacy of his apartment, where he posed single men and couples against a bare wall. There, the often-square format and a raking light that sculpts the shoulders lend the embraces a hushed gravity.

blocks.caption: Nashom holds Howard, NYC, 1994 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: Before this backdrop came, in Hancock’s words, “the artists, the friends, the porn stars, the lovers.” In Nashom holds Howard, NYC (1994), two hands clasp the brow of a young man, his eyes turned heavenward like a Saint Sebastian. These portraits sway between exhibition and introspection. In Jason, NYC (1990), the model offers himself naked and erect, one arm casually slung over the back of a leather armchair.

blocks.caption: Hugh Steers, NYC, 1993 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: The painter Hugh Steers, who depicted male intimacy in the age of the epidemic, poses for Stellar in 1993, folded in on himself, head bowed, ankles crossed above scuffed shoes. He would die of AIDS two years later, at 32. Of the hundreds of men who sat for him in those years, only a handful are still here. Yet in this book, Holleran writes, they “look out at you as if alive.”

blocks.caption: Canal Street Cigarette, 1976 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: Former models called Stellar after their diagnosis: “I am afraid I won’t look like this for long. Can I come back in?” Decades later, Hancock lingered over the picture of a beautiful young man glancing askance, eyes half rolled back. The photographer’s verdict was swift: “You can’t use that one.” Then he explained: “Because these are my friends. They were beautiful, but they are gone. I only want them to look their best.”

blocks.caption: Gay Pride Day, 1983 © Stanley Stellar 2026 courtesy Loose Joints

blocks.text: Don’t Worry Boys by Stanley Stellar is published by Loose Joints (2026).
